original_value: A good understanding of how meteorological conditions exacerbate or mitigate air pollution is critical for developing robust emission reduction policies. Thus, based on a multiple linear regression (MLR) model in this study, the quantified impacts of six meteorological variables on PM2.5 (i.e., particle matter with diameter of 2.5 µm or less) and its major components were estimated over the Yangtze River Basin (YRB). The 38-year (1980–2017) daily PM2.5 and meteorological data were derived from the newly-released Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis and Research and Application, version 2 (MERRA-2) products. The MERRA-2 PM2.5 was underestimated compared with ground measurements, partly due to the bias in the MERRA-2 Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) assimilation. An over-increasing trend in each PM2.5 component occurred for the whole study period; however, this has been curbed since 2007. The MLR model suggested that meteorological variability could explain up to 67% of the PM2.5 changes. PM2.5 was robustly anti-correlated with surface wind speed, precipitation and boundary layer height (BLH), but was positively correlated with temperature throughout the YRB. The relationship of relative humidity (RH) and total cloud cover with PM2.5 showed regional dependencies, with negative correlation in the Yangtze River Delta (YRD) and positive correlation in the other areas. In particular, PM2.5 was most sensitive to surface wind speed, and the sensitivity was approximately −2.42 µg m−3 m−1 s. This study highlighted the impact of meteorological conditions on PM2.5 growth, although it was much smaller than the anthropogenic emissions impact.

result.paraphrase: Using a multiple linear regression (MLR) model, this study estimated the quantified effects of six meteorological variables on PM2.5 (particle matter with a diameter of 2.5 µm or less) and its major components across the Yangtze River Basin (YRB). The analysis used 38 years of daily PM2.5 and meteorological data from the newly released Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis and Research and Application, version 2 (MERRA-2) products spanning 1980–2017. Compared with ground observations, MERRA-2 PM2.5 was underestimated, partly because of bias in the MERRA-2 Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) assimilation. Over the full study period, each PM2.5 component showed an over-increasing trend, though this trend has been restrained since 2007. The MLR results indicated that meteorological variability could account for as much as 67% of PM2.5 variation. PM2.5 was strongly negatively correlated with surface wind speed, precipitation, and boundary layer height (BLH), but positively correlated with temperature throughout the YRB. Relative humidity (RH) and total cloud cover had region-dependent relationships with PM2.5: negative in the Yangtze River Delta (YRD) and positive in other regions. PM2.5 was most sensitive to surface wind speed, with a sensitivity of about −2.42 µg m−3 m−1 s. Overall, the study emphasized that meteorological conditions affect PM2.5 growth, though their influence is much smaller than that of anthropogenic emissions.
